children: Geopolitical tensions, tariffs and disruptions to global supply chains are reshaping capital markets and creating fresh opportunities for India, particularly as multinational companies increasingly look at the country as a manufacturing base rather than merely a consumer market.

Sundeep Sikka, Managing Director & CEO, Nippon Life India Asset Management, said the forces influencing capital markets were moving beyond conventional economic policy towards geopolitics. Uncertainty over tariffs, ongoing conflicts, changing global alliances and shifts in energy markets were altering investment and business decisions worldwide.

“It’s no more ‘Make in India’; it is ‘built for the world in India’,” he said at an Association of Investment Bankers of India event here on Wednesday to highlighting the growing interest among foreign companies in establishing manufacturing operations in the country.

Recalling his recent participation in a delegation to Japan, Sikka said the nature of conversations with Japanese companies had changed significantly. Instead of having to explain India’s potential, discussions were increasingly focused on how companies could expand their operations in the country.
Interest was also coming from smaller companies, apart from large multinational corporations, indicating a broader reassessment of India’s role in global supply chains, he said.

Germany, too, could offer opportunities as manufacturing companies there explore locations outside the country amid changing business conditions, said Sikka, adding that India could emerge as an important destination for manufacturing-related capital.
He also pointed to growing strategic and economic engagement between India and other major economies, including Japan and Germany, as an indication of increasing trust in India’s economic potential.

At home, the growing participation of retail investors is emerging as an important structural change in India’s capital markets. Domestic investors were increasingly providing a counterbalance to dependence on foreign capital.

However, there remains considerable headroom for financial-market penetration. Only about 4 per cent of India’s population invests in mutual funds, compared with around 65 per cent globally while mutual fund assets account for about 16 per cent of GDP, he said.
Sikka also highlighted the strength of India’s primary market, pointing to the growing number of IPOs, investor appetite and the improving quality of companies accessing public markets.
He said the capital-markets ecosystem has an important role in connecting companies requiring capital with investors seeking to participate in India’s growth.
India is now at an “inflection point”, with domestic and foreign capital available alongside economic growth, he said.

title: ‘Built for the World in India’: Nippon AMC’s Sikka sees manufacturing opportunity amid global turmoil
